body.text: Why does History of Chile still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism that quietly governs liquidity, risk, and long-term purchasing power.

The territory of Chile has been populated since at least 13,000 BCE. By the 16th century, Spanish invaders began to raid the region of present-day Chile, and the territory was a colony from 1540 to 1818, when it gained independence from Spain.

The country's economic development was successively marked by the export of first agricultural produce, then saltpeter and later copper. The wealth of raw materials led to an economic upturn, but also led to dependency, and even wars with neighboring states.
Chile was governed during most of its first 150 years of independence by different forms of restricted government, where the electorate was carefully vetted and controlled by an elite.

body.text: Failure to address the economic and social increases and increasing political awareness of the less-affluent population, as well as indirect intervention and economic funding to the main political groups by the CIA, as part of the Cold War, led to a political polarization under Socialist president Salvador Allende.

This in turn resulted in the 1973 coup d'état and the military dictatorship of General Augusto Pinochet, whose seventeen-year regime was responsible for many human rights violations and deep market-oriented economic reforms. In 1990, Chile made a peaceful transition to democracy and initiated a succession of democratic governments.
Early history (13,000 BCE - 1540 CE)

There are various theories about how and when humans arrived in the Americas. It is generally agreed that people migrated from Asia to North America via the Bering Strait, which connected Siberia and Alaska.

The Coastal Migration Hypothesis posits that these humans then migrated southwards along the western coast of the Americas, thus populating Central and South America. Some archaeologists suspect multiple migrations may have taken place.

Researchers have proven that humans have lived in the valleys and coastal areas of what is now present-day Chile for at least 14,500 years. The archaeological site Monte Verde in southern Chile predates the well-known Clovis culture site in New Mexico by at least 1,000 years.
Evidence of early human settlements in Chile have been found in Cueva del Milodón and the Pali Aike Crater's lava tube.

Pre-Hispanic Chile was home to over a dozen different Indigenous societies, including Atacameños, Aymara, Chango, Chono, Qulla, Diaguita, Kawésqar, Mapuche, Quechua, Rapa Nui, Selk'nam, Tehuelche, and Yaghan communities. The largest Indigenous group in Chile was the Mapuche.
The Mapuche was composed of subgroups, such as the Picunche, the Araucanos, the Pehuenche, and the Huilliche, who lived in different environments and developed unique subcultures.

The Indigenous societies of Chile can be loosely grouped into three categories based on the climate they lived in: the Northern tribes of the Andes Mountains, the Mapuche in central-southern Chile, and the tribes of Patagonia.
The Mapuche - Central and Southern Chile
The Mapuche lived primarily off agriculture, with some communities using irrigation and others combining slash-and-burn agriculture with hunting.

The Incan Empire encountered fierce resistance when attempting to colonize Chile. During their attempts at conquest in 1460 and again in 1491, the Sapa Tupac Inca Yupanqui (c. 1471, 1493) and his army established forts in the Central Valley of Chile, but they were fought off by the Mapuche.

The result of the bloody three-day confrontation known as the Battle of the Maule was that the Inca conquest of the territories of Chile ended at the Maule river, which subsequently became the boundary between the Incan empire and the Mapuche lands until the arrival of the Spaniards.

5 million at most when the Spaniards arrived in the 1530s, a century of European conquest and disease reduced that number by at least half. During the conquest, the Araucanians quickly added horses and European weaponry to their arsenal of clubs and bows and arrows.
They became adept at raiding Spanish settlements and, albeit in declining numbers, managed to hold off the Spaniards and their descendants until the late 19th century.

The Araucanians' valor inspired the Chileans to mythologize them as the nation's first national heroes, a status that did nothing, however, to elevate the wretched living standard of their descendants.
Indigenous societies of Patagonia
The tribes of Patagonia include the Chonos, Kawésqar, Tehuelche, Selk'nam, Yagha. They were largely nomadic and supported themselves through fishing and hunting.
The name Patagonia comes from the word ] which was used by Magellan to describe the native people, whom he thought to be giants. 55 m (~5′1″) average for Spaniards of the time.

Patagonia is split between modern-day Chile and Argentina. The Argentine portion of Patagonia includes the provinces of Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz, as well as the eastern portion of Tierra del Fuego archipelago. The Argentine politico-economic Patagonic Region includes the Province of La Pampa.

The Chilean part of Patagonia includes the southern part of Valdivia, Los Lagos in Lake Llanquihue, Chiloé, Puerto Montt and the Archaeological site of Monte Verde, also the fiords and islands south to the regions of Aisén and Magallanes, including the west side of Tierra del Fuego and Cape Horn.
Indigenous societies of the Andes Mountains

The Indigenous societies who lived in the Andes Mountains or the Atacama Desert include the Atacameños, Aymara, Chango, Colla, and Quechua. They developed rich handicrafts and were influenced by pre-Incan cultures.

The Inca Empire briefly extended their empire into what is now northern Chile, where they collected tribute from small groups of fishermen and oasis farmers but were not able to establish a strong cultural presence in the area.
Spanish conquest and colonization (1520, 1810)

The first European in recorded history that saw Chilean territory was Ferdinand Magellan, who crossed the Strait of Magellan on November 1, 1520. However, Diego de Almagro is usually attributed with the colonization of Chile.

After leading the conquest of Peru with Francisco Pizarro, Almagro organized an expedition that brought him to central Chile in 1537. He did not find anything he considered valuable, so he returned to Peru.

After this initial excursion, Pedro de Valdivia, captain of the Spanish army, asked Pizarro's permission to invade and conquer the southern lands with the intent of expanding the Spanish Empire. With a couple of hundred men, he killed or forcefully displaced the Native inhabitants of central Chile.
He founded the city of Santiago de Nueva Extremadura, now Santiago de Chile, on February 12, 1541.

Although Valdivia found little gold in Chile, he was interested in the agricultural richness of the land. He continued his explorations of the region west of the Andes, founded over a dozen towns. He became the first governor of the Governorate of Chile.
In that post, he obeyed the viceroy of Peru and, through him, the King of Spain and his bureaucracy.

He established the first encomiendas, in which the Spanish Crown granted conquistadors land, and then conquistadors forced local Native people to pay tribute. As Valdivia and other colonizers encroached upon their land, Indigenous communities resisted.

The Mapuche were the most powerful opponents of the Spanish Empire, their military resistance to Spain became known as the Arauco War. This war lasted almost three centuries, and Spain never successfully subjugated the Mapuche territories. Valdivia died in 1553 at the Battle of Tucapel, defeated by Lautaro, a young Mapuche toqui (war chief).

The Great Uprising of 1598 swept all Spanish presence south of the Bío-Bío River except Chiloé (and Valdivia which was decades later reestablished as a fort), and the great river became the frontier line between Mapuche lands and the Spanish realm.
North of that line cities grew up slowly, and Chilean lands eventually became an important source of food for the Viceroyalty of Peru.

Responsible to the governor, town councils known as Cabildo administered local municipalities, the most important of which was Santiago, which was the seat of a Royal Appeals Court (Real Audiencia) from 1609 until the end of colonial rule.

Chile was the least wealthy realm of the Spanish Crown for most of its colonial history. Only in the 18th century did a steady economic and demographic growth begin, an effect of the reforms by Spain's Bourbon dynasty and a more stable situation along the frontier.
